questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Vertical Asymptotes for the Sum of Two Rational Functions
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's put the two terms over a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4x}-\frac{1}{x+5} & =\frac{x+5-4x}{4x(x+5)} \\  & =\frac{5-3x}{4x(x+5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we proceed to set the denominator equal to zero and get

$$
4x(x+5)=0\,⟹\,x=0\,,\,x=-5.
$$

Therefore, the vertical asymptotes are at $x=0$ and $x=-5.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying When a Rational Function has no Vertical Asymptotes
questions.worked_solution:
Let's simplify the expression by factoring both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-5)({x}^{3}+1)}{{x}^{2}-4x-5} & =\frac{(x-5)(x+1)({x}^{2}-x+1)}{(x-5)(x+1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-5)(x+1)}({x}^{2}-x+1)}{\cancel{(x-5)(x+1)}} \\  & ={x}^{2}-x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Since the denominator is never zero, we conclude that this function has no vertical asymptotes. A plot of the function is below. Note that it is not defined at $x=-1,$ and $x=5.$

questions.problem:
From **left to right**, the vertical asymptotes of $f(x)=\frac{1}{x-3}-\frac{1}{x+7}$ are

questions.worked_solution:
First, let's put the two terms over a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x-3}-\frac{1}{x+7} & =\frac{x+7-(x-3)}{(x-3)(x+7)} \\  & =\frac{10}{(x-3)(x+7)}\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we proceed to set the denominator equal to zero and get

$$
(x-3)(x+7)=0\,⟹\,x=-7\,,\,x=3.
$$

Therefore, from left to right, the vertical asymptotes are at $x=-7$ and $x=3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Vertical Asymptotes of Rational Functions by Factoring the Numerator and Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
We start by factoring the function as much as possible and canceling the common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{10x}{{x}^{2}+5x} & =\frac{10x}{x(x+5)} \\  & =\frac{10\cancel{x}}{\cancel{x}(x+5)} \\  & =\frac{10}{x+5}\end{aligned}
$$

We now set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
x+5=0\,⟹\,x=-5
$$

So the *only* vertical asymptote is at $x=-5.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Vertical Asymptotes of Rational Functions by Factoring the Numerator and Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
We start by factoring the function as much as possible and canceling the common factors:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-16}{{x}^{2}+6x+8} & =\frac{{x}^{2}-{4}^{2}}{(x+2)(x+4)} \\  & =\frac{(x-4)(x+4)}{(x+2)(x+4)} \\  & =\frac{(x-4)\cancel{(x+4)}}{(x+2)\cancel{(x+4)}} \\  & =\frac{x-4}{x+2}\end{aligned}
$$

We now set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
x+2=0\,⟹\,x=-2
$$

So the *only* vertical asymptote is at $x=-2.$
